slides.headline: He invented the DNA sequencing method that made a $200 human genome possible. It just won him a Wolf Prize.
Shankar Balasubramanian won the 2026 Wolf Prize in Chemistry, shared with David Klenerman and Pascal Mayer
slides.body: The Chennai-born chemist, now at the University of Cambridge, was recognized for inventing the Solexa/Illumina next-generation DNA sequencing method - the technology behind most of the world's genomic sequencing today.

slides.headline: A roughly million-fold drop in the cost and time of sequencing a genome.
slides.body: Their method helped make genome sequencing cheap and fast enough for everyday precision medicine - work that started in a lab, not a hospital, but ended up reshaping how diseases get diagnosed and treated worldwide.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: A Viksit Bharat needs scientists building the tools other scientists will use for decades.
slides.body: Balasubramanian's invention didn't just win him a prize - it became invisible infrastructure underneath a huge share of modern genomic medicine.
